youtube.title: Unpickable Lock: Who Finally Cracked London's 61-Year Challenge?
youtube.description:
The unpickable lock sat in a London shop window for 61 years, with a prize of 200 guineas for anyone who could pick it. Nobody could, until an American walked in.

It starts with a brass padlock from the Ann Francis, a ship wrecked off South Wales in 1583, whose letter code scientists just read with a micro CT scanner. Then we go back to the first wooden pin locks of the ancient world, Roman ring keys and medieval warded locks that a bent wire could beat. In 1790 Joseph Bramah put his challenge padlock in his Piccadilly window. In 1851, at the Great Exhibition, Alfred Charles Hobbs picked a Chubb detector lock in about 25 minutes, then spent about 51 hours over 16 days on the Bramah lock. And the key in your pocket? It is a 4,000-year-old idea.

In this video:
- The 1583 shipwreck padlock and its secret code
- Wooden pin locks, Roman ring keys and wards
- Bramah's 200 guinea challenge in the shop window
- Alfred Hobbs at the 1851 Great Exhibition
- Linus Yale and the pin tumbler key in your pocket

Subscribe to Stickstory for more everyday things with wild stories. What do you think the code A, N, C, E meant? Tell me in the comments!

#unpickablelock #lockpicking #historyoflocks #stickstory

scenes.text: This brass padlock spent more than four hundred years at the bottom of the sea.
scenes.visual: Underwater close-up: a crusted brass barrel padlock with four lettered rings and a U shackle lies half buried in the sand; light rays, rising bubbles, swaying seaweed and two small fish swim past; note '400 years underwater' on 'four'.

scenes.text: It came from the Ann Francis, a ship that wrecked off South Wales in 1583. And it was still locked.
scenes.visual: Underwater, wider: the broken wooden ribs of a wreck stick out of the sand; the small padlock lies in front of them; note 'Ann Francis, 1583'; red stamp 'STILL LOCKED' on 'locked'.

scenes.text: No keyhole, just rings of letters. So how do you open a lock when whoever knew the code died centuries ago?
scenes.visual: On a museum table with a blue cloth: the cleaned padlock, big, its four rings rolling through letters; the fez narrator stands at right and thinks, then holds up a sign 'CODE?' on 'code'.

scenes.text: Scientists at Cardiff University found out without even touching it. A micro CT scanner built a 3D picture of the inside.
scenes.visual: A lab: a big micro-CT scanner with a round bore; the padlock sits inside, a gold scan beam sweeps across it; on the monitor at right the x-ray of the inside fills in from left to right; note 'micro CT' on 'scanner'.

scenes.text: The notches lined up, and the code appeared: A, N, C, E.
scenes.visual: Close-up x-ray panel: inside the padlock four rings each show a gold notch that drifts up and down, then they line up with the locking bar on 'lined'; the letters A, N, C, E pop in gold above the rings one by one.

scenes.text: Here's the thing. Every lock ever made has a weakness.
scenes.visual: A London street: a Georgian shop front with a bow window; the fez narrator walks up to the window from the left and peers at the padlock through his spyglass on 'weakness'.

scenes.text: And for sixty-one years, one lock in a London shop window promised a fortune to anyone who could find it.
scenes.visual: The same shop front, closer: in the bow window a brass padlock sits on a red cloth stand with a card '200 GUINEAS'; a light glint sweeps across the glass; a red year counter runs 1790 to 1851 at top right.

scenes.text: Nobody could, until a man arrived from America. Who was he, and how did he do it?
scenes.visual: Full-frame old map of the North Atlantic: a red dashed route draws itself from Boston across the ocean to London on 'arrived'; a big red '?' pops up over London on 'Who'.

scenes.text: To answer that, we need to go way back.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 1 / 5 card: blue disc with 1, title 'The First Lock'.

scenes.text: Picture a door in the ancient world, with everything you own behind it. How do you keep it safe?
scenes.visual: Desert: a mud-brick storeroom with a palm tree; the wall is cut open at right showing clay jars and a small heap of gold; a wooden door with a wooden lock; the fez narrator stands at left, points at the jars on 'everything', then thinks on 'safe'.

scenes.text: One of the oldest locks ever found comes from the ruins of a palace at Khorsabad, in what is now Iraq. And it was made of wood.
scenes.visual: Full-frame old map from the Atlantic to Mesopotamia; a red dot and the name 'Khorsabad' pop up in northern Iraq on 'Khorsabad'; 'Egypt' and 'IRAQ' notes; red note 'made of wood' on 'wood'.

scenes.text: A wooden bolt slid across the door. When it closed, small wooden pins dropped into holes in the bolt and jammed it.
scenes.visual: Cutaway of an ancient wooden lock filling the frame: the door jamb at left, a wooden housing on the door with three pin channels, a long hollow bolt; on 'slid' the bolt slides left into the jamb; on 'dropped' three gold wooden pins drop into holes in the bolt; notes 'bolt' and red 'pins'.

scenes.text: To open it, you pushed in a big wooden key with pegs on top. The pegs lifted the pins, and the bolt slid free.
scenes.visual: Close-up of the same cutaway: a wooden key with three pegs slides into the hollow bolt from the right on 'pushed'; on 'lifted' the key rises and the pegs push the three pins up out of the bolt; on 'free' the bolt and key slide right; note 'key' and green 'free!'.

scenes.text: People call it the Egyptian lock, because it was so common in Egypt.
scenes.visual: Egypt: two pyramids on the horizon, a palm tree, a mud-brick storeroom; a wooden peg key slides into the wooden lock on the door and the bolt draws back; note 'the Egyptian lock' in red.

scenes.text: Remember those pins. But wood is clumsy. So what did the Romans do?
scenes.visual: Giant words 'Remember' / 'the pins' word by word, 'pins' in a red box; the fez narrator beside them points at the words on 'Remember', then shrugs on 'Romans'.

scenes.text: They made locks out of metal.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 2 / 5 card: blue disc with 2, title 'Iron and Wards'.

scenes.text: And they added wards: little ridges inside the lock that block any key without the right slots.
scenes.visual: Inside an iron lock case, front view: two curved iron ridges (wards) circle the keyhole; a red key with no slots turns and hits the ward on 'block' (red X); then a key with slots in its bit turns right past the wards on 'slots' and the bolt below slides.

scenes.text: Some Roman keys were so small that people wore them on their fingers as rings.
scenes.visual: Close-up: a hand rises into frame with a small bronze ring key on one finger, a gold sparkle on it; note 'Roman ring key' on 'rings'.

scenes.text: For centuries, locksmiths made beautiful iron locks with more and more wards.
scenes.visual: A medieval locksmith's forge: fire roaring in a brick hearth, a smith behind the anvil, a hammer swinging down on a glowing lock plate with sparks; keys swing on a wall rack; a round inset at right fills with five ward rings, one after another, on 'more'.

scenes.text: But here's the problem. Wards only block the key. They don't guard the bolt.
scenes.visual: Inside the iron lock case, the fez narrator drawn small stands on the floor of the cutaway next to the end of the bolt; on 'bolt' he pushes it along by hand and it slides open; red note 'bolt unguarded'.

scenes.text: A thief just needed a bent piece of metal that slipped around them.
scenes.visual: Night: a stone storeroom wall with a heavy wooden door and an iron lock plate; a lantern glows on the ground; a thief in a slouch hat crouches at the door and slides a thin red bent wire into the keyhole on 'bent'.

scenes.text: So a lock looked strong, but it was easy to beat.
scenes.visual: Close-up of the iron lock plate on the dark planks: the red bent wire wiggles in the keyhole; red stamp 'EASY TO BEAT' lands on 'easy'.

scenes.text: Then a London engineer decided to fix that for good.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 3 / 5 card: blue disc with 3, title 'The Challenge in the Window'.

scenes.text: His name was Joseph Bramah, and he patented his lock in 1784. It used a tiny tube-shaped key.
scenes.visual: Bramah's workshop: shelves of locks, a turning lathe wheel and belt, a workbench with sparks; a period engineer (no hat) works at the bench; the tiny tube-shaped key drawn big on the bench; notes 'Joseph Bramah', 'patent 1784', red 'tube key' on 'tube'.

scenes.text: Inside, sliders all had to be pushed to exactly the right depth at once. One slider off by a hair, and nothing turned.
scenes.visual: Close-up end view inside a Bramah lock: a big brass disc with eight radial sliders around a round core; the tube key enters and pushes the sliders, their notches meet a gold ring and turn green on 'depth'; on 'off' one slider overshoots and turns red, the core only shudders and a red X appears; the tube key drawn at right.

scenes.text: In 1790, Bramah was so sure of it that he put a padlock in his Piccadilly shop window, with a sign.
scenes.visual: Reverse angle from inside the dark shop: the back of the brass padlock on its red stand and the back of the sign card in the bow window; outside, a crowd of Londoners in hats press their faces to the glass and stare; note '1790'.

scenes.text: It said: The artist who can make an instrument that will pick or open this lock shall receive 200 guineas the moment it is produced.
scenes.visual: Close-up of the framed card from the window: lines of copperplate handwriting write themselves; on 'guineas' a big red '200 GUINEAS' lands; a small padlock drawing at lower right.

scenes.text: That was a fortune. Bramah died in 1814, and the lock was still waiting.
scenes.visual: The shop front at night under the gas lamp, window glowing; the red year counter ticks on from 1814 to 1817; red note 'still waiting'.

scenes.text: In 1818, after thieves used false keys at Portsmouth Dockyard, Jeremiah Chubb won a government prize with his detector lock.
scenes.visual: Portsmouth Dockyard at night under the moon: a brick storehouse with a big door, ships' masts behind; two thieves at the door, a ring of false keys jiggling in the lock on 'false'; notes 'Portsmouth Dockyard' and red 'Chubb wins, 1818' on 'Chubb'.

scenes.text: Lift a lever too high, and it jammed and gave the thief away.
scenes.visual: Close-up of the levers: the pick lifts one lever too high on 'high', the red detector drops and catches it, the bolt shudders; red stamp 'JAMMED' on 'jammed'.

scenes.text: So by 1851, London had two unpickable locks. But that summer, the whole world came to town.
scenes.visual: Giant words 'Two' / 'unpickable locks' word by word, 'unpickable' in a red box; the fez narrator holds up a sign '1851' and waves on 'world'.

scenes.text: The Great Exhibition opened in a giant hall of glass and iron: the Crystal Palace.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 4 / 5 card: blue disc with 4, title '1851: The Locksmith from Boston'.

scenes.text: Among the visitors was a locksmith from Boston named Alfred Charles Hobbs. He came to sell American locks. Instead, he picked one.
scenes.visual: Inside the Crystal Palace: glass-and-iron arches, a big elm tree, red and blue pennants swaying, a crowd of heads in front; a period man (Hobbs, short beard) walks in from the left and holds up a pick on 'picked'; notes 'Alfred C. Hobbs' and 'from Boston'.

scenes.text: In front of astonished onlookers, Hobbs opened a Chubb detector lock in about 25 minutes.
scenes.visual: A Westminster room with striped wallpaper and a tall curtained window: a table with a brass Chubb lock, Hobbs at the left picking it, onlookers at the right; a big clock at top right sweeps a red wedge as the counter climbs to '25 min'; on 'minutes' the bolt pops out and the onlookers jump.

scenes.text: When they asked him to do it again, he did it in seven.
scenes.visual: Same room, medium shot: the clock counter now runs only to '7 min'; the fez narrator, whole figure at right, jumps back in shock on 'seven'.

scenes.text: But the big prize was still in that shop window, so Hobbs took the challenge.
scenes.visual: Close-up at the bow window: Hobbs, big in the foreground at left, leans towards the glass and points at the brass padlock on its red stand on 'challenge'; red note 'challenge!'.

scenes.text: He could use any tools, but the lock had to survive unharmed.
scenes.visual: A room above the shop: the Bramah padlock clamped in a vice on a table, a row of thin picks laid out, an oil lamp flickering, a wall clock and a red day calendar; two picks wiggle in the keyhole; Hobbs stands at left watching; notes 'any tools' and red 'no damage'.

scenes.text: He worked for about 51 hours, spread over 16 days.
scenes.visual: Close on the table: the picks wiggle in the Bramah keyhole, the wall clock hands spin fast, the red calendar flips from DAY 1 to DAY 16; red note '51 hours'.

scenes.text: And then the lock opened. After sixty-one years, the unpickable lock was picked.
scenes.visual: Big close-up of the Bramah padlock with a pick in its keyhole; on 'opened' the shackle springs up with gold rays bursting round it; red stamp '61 YEARS' on 'sixty'.

scenes.text: Critics complained: no real burglar gets sixteen days alone with a lock. Fair point.
scenes.visual: A Victorian club room with green striped wallpaper, a portrait and a fire: a critic in a red armchair waves a newspaper with the headline '16 DAYS?'; a second critic points at it; the fez narrator at left thinks, then shrugs on 'Fair'.

scenes.text: But the lesson stuck: every lock can be picked. It's only a question of time. So what do you put on your door after that?
scenes.visual: Giant words 'Every lock' / 'can be picked' word by word, 'picked' in a red box; small note 'only a question of time' on 'time'.

scenes.text: The answer came from America, and it was very old.
scenes.visual: CHAPTER 5 / 5 card: blue disc with 5, title 'The Key in Your Pocket'.

scenes.text: In 1848, a locksmith named Linus Yale made a pin tumbler lock based on the Egyptian idea: pins that drop and jam, and a key that lifts them.
scenes.visual: Full-frame old map across the Atlantic: Egypt and Khorsabad in the east, London, and a red dashed route arcing across the ocean to Connecticut in America; notes 'Linus Yale, 1848' and 'the Egyptian idea'.

scenes.text: In the 1860s, his son, Linus Yale Junior, made it small. He put the pins in a little cylinder and shrank the big wooden key into flat metal with a jagged edge.
scenes.visual: Cutaway of a Yale pin tumbler cylinder filling the frame: a brass housing with five pin chambers, springs, grey driver pins and gold key pins; a flat key with a jagged edge slides in from the right on 'flat', its bumps lift the pins; notes 'Linus Yale Jr.' and 'cylinder'.

scenes.text: Each bump lifts one pin to exactly the right height, and the cylinder turns.
scenes.visual: Close-up of the pins: the key is fully in, every gap sits exactly on the shear line, which glows green; the key's bow turns on 'turns'; green note 'turns!'.

scenes.text: Go look at your front door key. Those bumps are pin heights.
scenes.visual: A front door of wooden planks with a round brass lock; a big modern flat key floats across the frame, and above each bump a gold pin rises on a dotted line up to a green line; the fez narrator at right points at the bumps on 'bumps'.

scenes.text: You carry a four thousand year old idea in your pocket. And yes, it can be picked too.
scenes.visual: Horizontal timeline: 'Khorsabad / wooden pins', 'Rome / ring keys', '1784 / Bramah', '1851 / Hobbs', '1860s / Yale'; the marker runs to Yale.

scenes.text: Which brings us back to Wales. The Ann Francis belonged to Francis Shaxton, a merchant said to be a smuggler, and the padlock probably guarded a chest.
scenes.visual: Inside the dark hold of a wooden ship: curved ribs, barrels; a sea chest with iron bands, the brass letter padlock swinging on its hasp; silver coins spill out onto the planks on 'smuggler'; notes 'Francis Shaxton' and red 'smuggler?'.

scenes.text: And nobody knows why its owner chose those four letters.
scenes.visual: Close-up of the padlock on the table: its four rings show A, N, C, E and glow, letter by letter.

scenes.text: So what do you think A, N, C, E meant? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe to Stickstory for more everyday things with wild stories.
scenes.visual: Medium shot: the fez narrator, big, stands next to the padlock on the table and turns its rings with his hand; they roll and stop on A N C E on 'think'; he holds up a sign 'ANCE = ?' and waves goodbye on 'subscribe'.
